read.sections.1.text.note: "The artist may have left some details out" became "pembuat gambar itu mungkin tidak menggambar semua detail" (the person who made the drawing), not "pelukis" (painter). The question after the colon is lower case, as usual in Indonesian.
read.sections.1.text.back: Different sources can answer different questions about the past. The receipt shows what a shop sold and the price of each item, so the receipt tells us that rice cost 12 tokens. The picture shows what the market looked like, with stalls, baskets and a cart. But the maker of the picture may not have drawn every detail. The diary tells what a young person saw and did on market day. It says that the traders came by boat before sunrise, but one person cannot see everything. So historians always ask two questions: what does this source tell me, and what can it not tell?
read.sections.1.text.source: Different sources can answer different questions about the past. The receipt shows what one shop sold and the price of each item, so it tells us that rice cost 12 tokens. The drawing shows what the market looked like, with stalls, baskets and a cart. However, the artist may have left some details out. The diary describes what one young person saw and did on market day. It says that traders arrived by boat before sunrise, but one person cannot see everything. So a historian always asks two questions: What does this source tell me, and what can it not tell me?

read.sections.2.text.note: "Together, these clues suggest" became "membuat kita menduga bahwa" (lead us to guess) to keep the tentative sense and avoid repeating "menunjukkan".
read.sections.2.text.back: One source almost never tells the whole story, so historians compare sources. Comparing means looking at two things and noticing what is the same and what is different. The picture shows a river, and the diary says that traders came by boat. Put together, these clues make us guess that the river helped people bring goods to the market. Historians also ask who made each source, and why it was made. Some questions are still unanswered, because no source tells us how many people lived in Riverstone. A strong claim explains what the evidence shows and what we still do not know.
read.sections.2.text.source: One source almost never tells the whole story, so historians compare sources. To compare means to look at two things and notice how they are similar or different. The drawing shows a river, and the diary says that traders came by boat. Together, these clues suggest that the river helped people bring goods to the market. A historian also asks who made each source, and why they made it. Some questions stay open, because none of the sources tells us how many people lived in Riverstone. A strong claim explains what the evidence shows and what we still do not know.

read.sections.0.heading.back: Sources are clues about the past
read.sections.0.heading.source: Sources are clues about the past

read.sections.0.text.back: No one alive now has ever seen the world as it was 1,000 years ago, so how can we know about that time? A historian is a person who studies the past by looking for sources. A source is anything that gives us information about the past. Letters, photos, pictures, tools, receipts, buildings and maps can be sources, and so can memories told by older people. Each source is like a clue in a puzzle. The picture, the receipt and the diary from Riverstone are three sources about one market. Historians use clues like these as evidence, then make claims about what happened.
read.sections.0.text.note: "pernah melihat dunia seperti 1.000 tahun yang lalu" can read as "saw the world, like, 1,000 years ago". Consider "pernah melihat seperti apa dunia 1.000 tahun yang lalu".
read.sections.0.text.source: Nobody alive today saw the world as it was 1,000 years ago, so how do we know about it? A historian is a person who studies the past by looking for sources. A source is anything that gives us information about the past. Letters, photographs, drawings, tools, receipts, buildings and maps can all be sources, and so can memories that older people share. Each source is like a clue in a puzzle. The Riverstone drawing, receipt and diary are three sources about one market. A historian uses clues like these as evidence and then makes a claim about what happened.

read.sections.0.simpler.back: No one now saw the world of long ago. So how can we know? A historian is a person who studies the past. Historians look at sources. Sources tell us something about the past. A source can be a letter, a photo or a tool. A source can also be a story from an older person. Each source is a clue. We use clues as evidence. Evidence helps us make claims about the past.

write.example.back: In my opinion, Riverstone Market used to be a busy place, where people bought and sold food. The picture shows stalls selling food and cloth. The picture also shows people carrying baskets. The diary also shows that the market was busy. It says that the traders came by boat before sunrise. Put together, these sources give a clue that the river helped traders bring goods to the market. But those sources do not tell us how many people lived in Riverstone. Those sources also do not tell us what the market was like on other days.
write.example.note: "sumber-sumber ini menunjukkan bahwa sungai membantu" states as fact what the English only suggests; the lesson teaches hedged claims. Consider "memberi petunjuk bahwa" or adding "mungkin" (as the simpler reading does), to match whatever is chosen for sentenceStarters.3. | Fixed after review: the example now hedges ("give a clue that") as the English "suggest" does.
write.example.source: I think Riverstone Market was a busy place where people traded food. The drawing shows stalls selling food and cloth. It also shows people carrying baskets. The diary also shows that the market was crowded. It says traders came by boat before sunrise. Together, these sources suggest that the river helped traders bring goods to the market. But the sources do not tell us how many people lived in Riverstone. They also do not tell us what the market was like on other days.

watch.summary.back: This short video explains primary sources. A primary source is made at the time you are studying, often by a person who was there at the time. Letters, diaries, photos, receipts, maps and tools can be primary sources. A primary source does not have to be famous or special. An everyday shopping receipt can show what people bought and how much it cost. A diary can show what one person saw and felt. But each primary source only shows part of the story. So historians ask who made it, when and why. Then they compare it with other sources. In this lesson, the picture, the receipt and the diary are all primary sources. Put together, the three tell us more than one source alone.

A diary can show what one person saw and felt. But each primary source shows only part of the story. So historians ask who made it, when, and why. Then they compare it with other sources. In this lesson, the drawing, the receipt and the diary are all primary sources. Together, they tell us more than any one of them alone.
